extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and students of philosophy/logic of science (readers of The Popular Science Monthly)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying and judging types of synthetic inference (induction, hypothesis, deduction) and choosing appropriate reasoning methods for different sciences; includes psychological/physiological analogies and practical heuristics. Useful for assessing arguments and methods in scientific writing or reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between induction and hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction infers from one set of facts to another set of similar facts; hypothesis infers from facts of one kind to facts of another kind. Induction is a stronger kind of inference than hypothesis. Hypotheses often assert facts not capable of direct observation (example: the historical existence of Napoleon), and cannot in essence be replaced by induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the core test: does the inference move between similar kinds of facts (induction) or from one kind to another (hypothesis)? Beware of the anti-pattern of 'distorting' hypothetic inferences into the appearance of induction by rephrasing them as predictions of future facts similar to observed ones. Example given: inferring Napoleon's historical existence is hypothetic because observed confirming facts may be of different kinds (e.g., future unimagined evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Essence of induction: inference of rules (habit formation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essence of an induction is that it infers a rule from observed facts; such a rule corresponds to a habit. Belief in a general rule is of the nature of a habit, and induction is the logical formula expressing the physiological process of habit formation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating inductive arguments, check whether they warrant inferring a general rule (habit) from the particular observations. Consider the strength of the habit-analogy: how reliably similar future observations are expected to follow past ones. The passage ties logical strength of induction to its role in forming stable, general beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis as sensuous/emotional conception
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis substitutes a single, intense conception for a complicated tangle of predicates attached to a subject, producing a peculiar sensuous element of thought (emotion). A hypothetic inference commonly involves the formation of such an emotion/feeling and often infers facts not directly observable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that hypotheses often provide vivid, unified pictures that explain disparate facts; evaluate them not only for empirical support but for their tendency to produce a strong sensuous conviction. Be cautious that appealing emotional vividness is not by itself proof; it is characteristic but not decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction as attention/volitional element
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduction adds nothing new to the premises but selects one of the represented facts and directs attention to it; it is the logical formula for paying attention and corresponds to a volitional/nervous discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appraising deductive reasoning, check that conclusions are legitimately drawn from premises without illicit addition. Understand deduction's role as clarifying or focusing consequences of accepted premises rather than generating new empirical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of sciences by dominant mode of reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Sciences can be classified by their predominant mode of inference: classificatory sciences are purely inductive (systematic botany, zoology, mineralogy, chemistry); sciences of theory (e.g., astronomy, pure physics) occupy a different place; sciences of hypothesis include disciplines like geology and biology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply reasoning methods appropriate to the discipline: expect taxonomy/induction in classificatory fields, theoretical (possibly mathematical) treatments in theory sciences, and hypothesizing in fields where unobservables and explanatory stories are central. This classification can guide methodological expectations and evaluation criteria for work in each field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical heuristic: assess whether an inference is induction or hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Habitually consider whether a given 'inference' belongs to induction or hypothesis (the two forms of synthetic inference). Doing so offers practical advantages in reasoning and scientific practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the routine of classifying inferences as inductive or hypothetic when reading or producing scientific arguments; this helps avoid category errors and clarifies what kind of support or evidence is appropriate. The author promises various practical benefits from this habit of mind.
